intro: The Andante con moto, the second movement of the Unfinished Symphony, D. 759, opens in E major with horns, bassoons and pizzicato basses. The opening material is interrupted several times by a minor-key woodwind melody, each time followed by the full orchestra.

sections.label: A · Horns and bassoons; theme in E major
sections.mNote: Long string phrases develop from a two-bar wind figure.

sections.label: B · Second theme in C♯ minor, clarinet
sections.mNote: Four violin notes lead in; clarinet, then oboe, plays the melody.

sections.label: A′ · Opening string theme in E major
sections.mNote: The opening theme returns after the full-orchestra outburst.

sections.label: B′ · Oboe theme in A minor
sections.mNote: Oboe and clarinet exchange their earlier roles

sections.label: Coda · Opening figure, then A♭ major
sections.mNote: Woodwinds take the first theme into A♭ major.

cues.title: Opening phrase, horns and bassoons
cues.text: Horns and bassoons play a two-bar phrase over pizzicato double basses. The strings follow with a long melody in E major. The opening two bars return at the end of the movement.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1885), second movement, p. 19; opening cadential figure and its final return described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Wolfgang Stähr on the Andante
cues.text: Wolfgang Stähr heard this Andante as a leave-taking without return. He pointed to the horn fifths, the bass lines, the string melodies with their cadences, and clarinet and oboe solos that “sound like farewells from songs of travel”.
cues.evidence: Wolfgang Stähr, Berliner Philharmoniker programme note on Symphony No. 7 (8) in B minor, D 759, on the Andante. https://www.berliner-philharmoniker.de/en/programme-notes/franz-schubert-symphony-no-7-in-b-minor-d-759-unfinished
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Hanslick’s review, Vienna, 1865
cues.text: Reviewing the Vienna première in 1865, Eduard Hanslick heard “musical thunder clouds” crossing the Andante. He wrote of how much Schubert achieved with a few horn figures and a clarinet or oboe solo.
cues.evidence: Eduard Hanslick’s review of the first performance (17 December 1865), in Henry Pleasants’s translation, Music Criticisms 1846–99 (Penguin, 1963; Dover, 1988): the Andante’s hints of complaint have the effect of “musical thunder clouds rather than of dangerous clouds of passion”, and with “a few horn figurations and here and there a clarinet or oboe solo” Schubert achieves tonal effects that “no refinement of Wagnerian instrumentation can capture”.

cues.title: Second subject, clarinet and oboe
cues.text: The first violins play four bare notes outlining C♯ minor. The clarinet begins the second melody in that key, and the oboe continues it in C♯ major.
cues.evidence: Second movement, transition to the second subject and the clarinet–oboe exchange. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Piano short score
cues.text: Schubert drafted the symphony first as a piano short score. The draft of this movement survives complete, with the end of the first movement and a scherzo that stops partway through its trio. After his death it passed to his brother Ferdinand; no draft of a finale has been found.
cues.evidence: Benjamin-Gunnar Cohrs, “Schuberts Unvollendete: Eine Bestandsaufnahme” (2008), preface to his edition of the scherzo D 759/3 with Nicola Samale, summarising the Neue Schubert-Ausgabe (1996): the piano draft of at least three movements, its first three of ten pages (the first 248 bars of the first movement) lost, the scherzo draft ending with the trio; the draft passing to Ferdinand Schubert, in 1859 to Nicolaus Dumba, and in 1901 to the archive of the Gesellschaft der Musikfreunde. Translation ours. https://repertoire-explorer.musikmph.de/wp-content/uploads/vorworte_prefaces/884.html

cues.title: Full orchestra in C♯ minor
cues.text: The full orchestra takes over in C♯ minor. Its closing passage reaches D♭ major, the same sounding tonic as C♯ major but written with flats. A short bridge leads back to E major.
cues.evidence: Second movement, closing group and transition to the recapitulation. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the opening theme
cues.text: The opening theme returns in E major after the full orchestra has played the closing theme. The strings play long phrases, and the winds reply.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1885), second movement, recapitulation; formal account at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Victor release on three discs
cues.text: Victor issued Stokowski’s recording of the symphony on three discs, 6663 to 6665, gathered in an album. Six matrices, recorded on 28 and 30 April 1927, supplied the six record sides for the two movements.
cues.evidence: Pristine Classical PASC 483: matrices CVE 29052-6 to 29057-7, recorded 28 and 30 April 1927, first issued on Victor 6663–6665 in album M-16. https://www.pristineclassical.com/products/pasc483

cues.title: Second subject in A minor, oboe
cues.text: The second subject returns in A minor, a major third lower than its earlier C♯ minor. This time the oboe begins and the clarinet continues, which reverses their earlier roles.
cues.evidence: Second movement, second subject in the recapitulation: A minor, oboe followed by clarinet. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Coda on the opening figure
cues.text: The two-bar phrase that opened the movement becomes the first melody of the coda. Schubert extends it at length before the final return to E major.
cues.evidence: Second movement, coda: extension of the opening two-bar E-major cadential figure. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Coda, woodwinds in A♭ major
cues.text: In the coda the woodwinds play the first theme in A♭ major, a key far removed from E. The short violin transition figure follows, and the movement ends in E major.
cues.evidence: Second movement, coda: woodwind restatement in A♭ major, violin transition motto and E-major conclusion. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Grove’s proposed finale
cues.text: A finale in B minor would normally follow. Soon after Herbeck found the score, George Grove suspected that the long entr’acte in B minor that Schubert wrote for Rosamunde in 1823 was meant for it. Brian Newbould and others have since argued the case.
cues.evidence: Benjamin-Gunnar Cohrs, “Schuberts Unvollendete: Eine Bestandsaufnahme” (2008): Grove’s early suggestion of the Rosamunde Entr’acte in B minor (D 797/1) as the finale, and Newbould’s argument that its two-strand development is symphonic rather than theatrical. Translation ours. https://repertoire-explorer.musikmph.de/wp-content/uploads/vorworte_prefaces/884.html

cues.title: Scherzo fragment in the manuscript
cues.text: The full score ends with this close in E major. On the back of its last page the manuscript continues into a scherzo in B minor, orchestrated for only a few bars before it breaks off. The title page is dated 30 October 1822, and Schubert lived another six years.
cues.evidence: Cohrs, “Schuberts Unvollendete: Eine Bestandsaufnahme” (2008): the 70-page fair copy, its title page “Sinfonia in H moll von Franz Schubertmpia … Wien den 30. Octob. 1822”, and the scherzo breaking off after a few orchestrated bars. Phillip Huscher, “The mystery of Schubert’s ‘Unfinished’ Symphony”, Chicago Symphony Orchestra (2021): nine bars of the scherzo, fully scored, on the back of the Andante’s last page. Schubert died on 19 November 1828. https://repertoire-explorer.musikmph.de/wp-content/uploads/vorworte_prefaces/884.html https://chicagosymphony.org/inside-the-music/article/7349/the-mystery-of-schuberts-unfinished-symphony

transitions.title: Four unaccompanied violin notes
transitions.from: A · Horns and bassoons; theme in E major
transitions.to: B · Second theme in C♯ minor, clarinet
transitions.how: After the E-major first theme, the first violins play four unaccompanied notes that outline C♯ minor. The clarinet then takes up the new melody in that key, and the oboe continues it in C♯ major.
transitions.evidence: Second movement, first-violin transition and second subject. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert)

transitions.title: Return to E major after the closing theme
transitions.from: B · Second theme in C♯ minor, clarinet
transitions.to: A′ · Opening string theme in E major
transitions.how: The full orchestra plays the closing theme, which ends in D♭ major. A short transition brings the music back to E major. The strings then take up the opening melody again, and the winds reply to them.
transitions.evidence: Second movement, closing group and recapitulation. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert)

transitions.title: The oboe takes the clarinet’s melody
transitions.from: A′ · Opening string theme in E major
transitions.to: B′ · Oboe theme in A minor
transitions.how: The second melody returns in A minor, a major third below its first appearance. The oboe plays the opening phrase and the clarinet continues, the reverse of their earlier order.
transitions.evidence: Second movement, second subject in the recapitulation. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert)

transitions.title: Opening cadence extended into the coda
transitions.from: B′ · Oboe theme in A minor
transitions.to: Coda · Opening figure, then A♭ major
transitions.how: The full-orchestra closing passage dies down. The two-bar cadential figure in E major from the opening is extended into a new melody for the coda. The violin motto, heard later, takes this melody on towards the woodwinds’ A♭-major restatement.
transitions.evidence: Second movement, coda and its derivation from the opening cadence. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._8_(Schubert)

source.title: Schubert, Symphonie in H moll (unvollendet), Schubert’s Werke, Serie 1 Nr. 8 (Leipzig: Breitkopf & Härtel, 1885)
source.locator: IMSLP #73284, second movement, Andante con moto, printed pages 19–31.

timeline.note: Bassoons and horns sound the two-bar opening phrase over plucked basses.
The strings begin their long E-major melody; the winds answer.
Four unaccompanied violin notes outline C♯ minor.
The solo clarinet begins the second melody in C♯ minor.
The solo oboe continues the melody in C♯ major.
The full orchestra interrupts with the closing theme.
The strings return to the opening E-major melody.
Oboe begins the second melody in A minor; clarinet follows.
The closing theme returns in the full orchestra.
Clarinets, bassoons and bass trombone play the first theme in A♭ major over soft strings.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The performing edition and any cuts or retouchings by the conductor are not identified in the sources consulted.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.value: 28 and 30 April 1927: part 1 on 28 April, parts 2 and 3 on 30 April
fields.note: Bolig dates CVE-29055 (part 1) to 28 April 1927 and CVE-29056 and CVE-29057 (parts 2 and 3) to 30 April 1927; the Internet Archive description and Pristine give the two session days for the symphony. Bolig calls the movement “Allegro con moto”; the usual marking is Andante con moto.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Academy of Music, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Stokowski’s earlier acoustic recording of 1924 used the same matrix numbers without the CVE prefix and different issue numbers (Bolig lists 74894–74897 and 6459–6460); this transfer is the electrical recording of 1927 by its description, session dates and Victor numbers.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The Internet Archive description says “Originally issued as Victor 6663, 6664 & 6665. (Later as a set as M-16.)”; Pristine gives the same numbers and album. Bolig also lists later Victor and HMV issues of the same sides. The disc and side on which the movement boundary falls are not identified; the allocation of matrices to movements follows Bolig’s part numbers.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Parts 1–3: CVE-29055, take 7 (Bolig) or take 6 (Pristine); CVE-29056, take 7; CVE-29057, take 7
fields.note: The two discographic sources agree on the matrices and on takes 7 for CVE-29056 and CVE-29057 but differ on the take of CVE-29055. Neither can be checked against a label image here, and the DAHR matrix pages could not be opened on 17 October 2026 (503 error).

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: The Internet Archive description reads “Transfer by Bob Varney”.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: No transfer date is identified. The Internet Archive item was added on 24 January 2011, which is an upload date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: The stylus, equalisation, speed and noise treatment are not documented. The file runs 11:55; Pristine’s own restoration runs 12:00, so the two transfers differ by a few seconds, and where the side joins fall in this file is not known.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Schubert died in 1828. This is a term calculation, not a worldwide clearance or a statement about an unidentified modern edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial: sound recording public domain in the European Union (pre-1963 publication basis).
fields.note: The Internet Archive item carries a CC0 licence URL declared by the uploader, which is not treated as authority to waive Victor’s rights. The pre-1963 European rule applies because the recording was made in 1927 and was on sale by January 1928 (a Victor advertisement in The Golden Book Magazine offers Records Nos. 6663-4-5), so the 50-year term expired before the 2013 extension; the exact first issue date is not established. This is territorial, not a worldwide licence. The recording was published after 1925, so a US public-domain basis is not established.
alts: Pre-1963 European public domain — territorial basis.
CC0 — licence URL on the Internet Archive item, uploader’s declaration.

composer.epithet: Composer who at seventeen wrote a song for Gretchen with a spinning-wheel accompaniment and at thirty-one wrote music for two cellos.
facts: Vienna Stadtkonvikt, 1808–13; composition lessons with Antonio Salieri
School assistant; tutor to the Esterházy daughters at Zseliz in 1818 and 1824; independent composer
The singer Vogl, the poets Schober and Mayrhofer, the painter Schwind, Josef von Spaun
More than 600 songs; symphonies, chamber music, piano sonatas and duets, masses and stage works

quote.text: I like these songs more than all the others, and you will come to like them too.
quote.source: Schubert to his friends about Winterreise, 1827, as Josef von Spaun later recalled; our translation

composer.background:
In the Schubert family quartet, Franz played the viola, his brothers the violins and his father the cello. He was born on 31 January 1797 in Himmelpfortgrund, a Viennese suburb, and grew up in his father’s schoolhouse. His father taught him violin, his brother Ignaz piano, and the parish musician Michael Holzer taught him further. At eleven he entered the imperial chapel choir and the Stadtkonvikt boarding school, where he played Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven in the school orchestra.

Salieri began teaching him composition in 1812. The next year Schubert left the boarding school, trained as a teacher and returned to his father’s classroom as an assistant. On 19 October 1814, aged seventeen, he wrote Gretchen am Spinnrade. In the piano part the right hand imitates the spinning wheel and the left hand the treadle, while Goethe’s Gretchen sings of her thoughts of Faust. At the point where she recalls his kiss, the accompaniment figure stops. The following year brought roughly 140 songs, among them Erlkönig, as well as church music, a symphony and works for the stage.
